It is the same eternal speech, already directed toward him in advance.
Al-Juwaynī, known as Imām al-Ḥaramayn and one of the leading Ashʿaris, who died in 478 AH / 1085 CE, summarized the position like this:
“We allow that a nonexistent person may be commanded on the assumption that he will exist. Once he exists, it becomes actual that he is commanded.”
Because the Ashʿaris affirmed God’s attributes and their eternity, Abū al-Ḥasan al-Ashʿarī, founder of the school, said that God:
just as He wills through an eternal will.
It has been established that God is a king.
A king is one who commands and forbids.
His command must then be either eternal or something that comes into existence.
If it comes into existence, it must arise either in God Himself, in some other place, or in no place at all.
It cannot arise in God Himself, because that would make God a place in which new events occur, and this is impossible.
It cannot arise in another place, because then that place would become the thing described by the command.
And it cannot arise in no place, because that is unintelligible.
Therefore God’s command must be eternal, existing in Him as one of His attributes.
“His speech is one. It is command, prohibition, report, question, promise and threat.
“These different descriptions arise from the different ways in which His single speech is considered. They do not mean that the speech itself is divided into many separate things.
“The expressions and words revealed through the angels to the prophets and messengers are signs pointing to the eternal speech.
“The sign is created and comes into existence, while what it points to is eternal.

“The difference between reading and what is read, and between recitation and what is recited, is like the difference between the person who remembers something and the thing remembered. The one remembering is created; the thing remembered may be eternal.”
Al-Shahrastānī gives us this Ashʿari theory in the passage above.
Abū al-Ḥasan al-Ashʿarī himself explains it in another way that brings out more clearly the distinction between inner speech and spoken speech.
His explanation also shows the more developed style of theological argument found in his period.
Al-Ashʿarī says that the word “speech” can be used in two ways, just as it can in human beings.
A human being can be called a speaker because he produces sound.
But we also speak of a kind of “speech within the self”—something that is neither sound nor letters.
This is the meaning present in the mind or self that spoken words later express.
When we move from human beings to God, al-Ashʿarī says, the same distinction applies.
There is an inner meaning belonging to God Himself.
It does not change when different expressions are used for it, and it does not become different when represented by different signs.
This is what Ashʿaris mean when they say that God’s speech is eternal.
It is God’s speech in the true sense.
The Qurʾān as something read and written, however, is unquestionably something that came into existence and was created, just as the Muʿtazilites say.
Every spoken word ends as soon as the next word is pronounced.
Each word therefore comes into existence in time, and the complete sequence formed from those words does as well.
The written and recited Qurʾān can still be called “the speech of God,” but only figuratively rather than literally.
There is something valuable and surprisingly deep in this Ashʿari discussion of human speech.
Whatever we may think of its metaphysical foundation, it comes fairly close in some respects to modern discussions of the relationship between language and thought.
It also begins from concrete human experience rather than from a purely metaphysical world.
But al-Shahrastānī reports an even deeper Muʿtazilite treatment of the relationship between language and thought, one that comes closer to the scientific reality of that relationship.
Speaking for the Muʿtazilites, he writes:
“We do not deny the thoughts that arise within a person’s mind. We may sometimes call them inner speech.
“But in reality, these thoughts are anticipations of the expressions that the tongue will later pronounce.
“A person who does not know a single word of Arabic does not have Arabic speech arising in his mind.
“The thoughts and inner conversations a person has depend on the expressions he learned from the beginning of his development.
“Those expressions are the basis from which the thoughts arise and to which they return.
“We therefore know that real speech is the ordered letters pronounced by the tongue.
“Among speakers of a language and among rational people generally, what comes from the tongue is what is normally called speech.
“Someone who can produce it is called a speaker; someone who cannot is called mute.
“This shows that speech is not in itself a separate rational essence or category like other abstract meanings.
“It consists of expressions, words and similar signs, and these differ according to convention, agreement and common usage.
“If a group of people agreed instead to communicate through taps, gestures or symbols, they could understand one another through these just as they understand one another through words.”
To pose the relationship between language and thought in this way shows a remarkable degree of theoretical awareness among the Muʿtazilites.
For a modern researcher, it is striking evidence of how important and innovative their contribution to knowledge was in their own time.
Before leaving the question of the created Qurʾān, however, we should record one final point about the Ashʿari current.
Despite its Salafi roots, it used rational methods just as the Muʿtazilites did.
C — The Question of Seeing God
This is another issue on which the Muʿtazilites took a distinctive position because of their rational understanding of divine unity and, in turn, their denial of separate divine attributes.
The denial that God can be seen is therefore a consequence of a consequence of their basic principle.
Even so, it became an important issue both for the Muʿtazilites and for their opponents and generated a great deal of theoretical debate.
The question concerns whether God can be seen with the physical eyes on the Day of Resurrection.
The Muʿtazilites denied this, despite Qurʾānic verses whose literal wording seems to suggest it.
“Faces on that day will be radiant, looking toward their Lord.” (Sūrat al-Qiyāma, verses 22–23)
The source of the Muʿtazilite position is clear.

As al-Shahrastānī says, they wanted to remove from God every possible resemblance to created things: direction, place, form, body, spatial position, movement, disappearance, change and being affected.
They therefore considered it necessary to reinterpret the ambiguous verses that seemed to suggest otherwise.
To see God with the eyes would obviously require Him to have a direction, a place, a body and so on.
Without such things, visual sight is impossible.
But all of these would contradict the Muʿtazilite understanding of divine unity.
The Muʿtazilites therefore reinterpreted the Qurʾānic verses whose literal wording appears to allow the sight of God.
“Faces on that day will be radiant, looking toward their Lord.”
They argued that “looking” here means waiting, expecting and hoping for God’s pardon and mercy.
Al-Zamakhsharī follows this interpretation in his commentary and supports it by an example from ordinary speech.
“At noon in Mecca, when people had closed their doors and gone inside to rest, I heard a woman begging and saying: ‘My little eyes are looking toward God and toward you.’
“What she meant was that the people of the Resurrection expect blessing and honour from no one but their Lord, just as in this world they feared and hoped in no one but Him.”
Al-Ashʿarī reports that the Muʿtazilites were unanimous that God:
They disagreed, however, over whether He could be “seen by the heart.”
Abū al-Hudhayl al-ʿAllāf and most Muʿtazilites said that we do see God with our hearts, meaning simply that we know Him through our hearts.
The Muʿtazilites also found Qurʾānic support for their rational rejection of physical vision.
“Eyes do not grasp Him, but He grasps all eyes.” (Sūrat al-Anʿām, verse 103)
Two Muʿtazilites belonging to al-Naẓẓām’s school, Aḥmad ibn Khābiṭ and al-Faḍl al-Ḥadathī, approached the problem through Neoplatonism.
Like the other Muʿtazilites, they denied that God Himself could be seen.
But they interpreted prophetic traditions that speak of seeing God in a different way.
“You will see your Lord on the Day of Resurrection just as you see the full moon, without crowding one another in order to see Him.”
They argued that what will actually be seen is the First Intellect, the first thing brought into existence, which is also the Active Intellect.
